name: Consensus

subjectOf.text: Contemporary corporate governance reforms are unlikely to work as policymakers and regulators intend, because experts agree improvement is needed but disagree widely on what good corporate governance is or how to achieve it.
subjectOf.abstract: Contemporary corporate governance reforms are unlikely to work as intended by policymakers and regulators.
subjectOf.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

subjectOf.text: Blockchain's distributed consensus model permits node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties, which makes it arguably safer than a traditional model requiring third party intermediary validation.
subjectOf.abstract: That model also allows node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties and is therefore arguably safer than a traditional model that requires third-party intermediary validation of transactions.
subjectOf.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: blockchains using node based distributed consensus

subjectOf.text: Blockchain's distributed consensus model, in which network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
subjectOf.abstract: Blockchain's distributed consensus model, e.g., the network "nodes" verify and validate chain transactions before execution of the transactions, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: distributed consensus models with node verification prior to execution

subjectOf.text: A government cannot control a blockchain by pressuring individuals within its territory; it would need complete control of 51 percent of the anonymous global users before it could change any part of the code.
subjectOf.abstract: If the U.S. government attempted to exert power over the system by influencing any number of individuals within their jurisdiction, they would need complete control of 51% of the anonymous global users before they could change any part of the code.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: decentralized public blockchains

subjectOf.text: Even if courts were given authority to order changes to smart contract code, a programmer coerced by a court could not override the will of the majority of anonymous international blockchain users to make an effective change.
subjectOf.abstract: Even if courts were given such authority, no programmer so coerced by the court would be able to override the will of the majority of anonymous international blockchain users to make an effective change.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: decentralized blockchains maintained by an anonymous global user majority

subjectOf.text: In the decentralized DLT model, distributed consensus replaces the trusted central validation system, substituting cryptographic solutions and economic incentives for a central validator.
subjectOf.abstract: In the decentralized DLT model, "distributed consensus" replaces the trusted central validation system.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908

subjectOf.text: A healthy expertise will have near unanimous consensus on every evidence of work validation pool, and that very unanimity creates an impediment to development, because honest members risk their stakes by voting for untested changes.
subjectOf.abstract: A healthy expertise will continually have near-unanimous consensus on every evidence-of-work validation pool. This creates an impediment to development.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Secure Proof of Stake Protocol (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125827
scope_conditions: well functioning expertise where all members run the same validated algorithms

subjectOf.text: Running the reputation platform on the very blockchain it validates destabilizes the system because it increases the likelihood of forks: every validation pool result is itself a transaction that must be included in a future block requiring its own validation, without end. The authors judge this destabilization non catastrophic for most imagined uses.
subjectOf.abstract: But this self-referential architecture destabilizes the system as it increases the likelihood of forks.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Secure Proof of Stake Protocol (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125827
scope_conditions: platform DApp hosted on the same chain it validates

subjectOf.text: Peer-to-peer transactions are possible because a distributed consensus model has network nodes verify, validate and audit transactions before and after execution, and this is often safer than routing transactions through a single trusted third-party intermediary.
subjectOf.abstract: "Peer-to-peer" transactions are possible because the technology uses a "distributed consensus model" where the network "nodes" verify, validate and audit transactions before and after they are executed.
subjectOf.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Why 'Blockchain' Will Disrupt Corporate Organizations (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3227933

subjectOf.text: Meaningful and secure reputation tokens supply the incentives needed for secure proof of stake consensus in block production, which eliminates the unsustainable inefficiencies of proof of work based blockchains.
subjectOf.abstract: giving the proper incentives for guaranteeing secure proof-of- stake consensus protocols for block production. This eliminates the unsustainable inefficiencies of proof-of-work based blockchains.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Gopinath Sivalingam, Reputation Protocol for the Internet of Trust - Conceptual Whitepaper (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3266953
scope_conditions: tokens that represent reputation per type of expertise

subjectOf.text: Semada replaces fungible currency staking with reputation staking for block propagation, a consensus algorithm the authors call Semada Proof of Reputation.
subjectOf.abstract: Block propagation in the Semada platform is facilitated by staking reputation, not a fungible currency as in PoS. Accordingly, the consensus algorithm is called Semada Proof of Reputation (PoR).
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Gopinath Sivalingam, Reputation Protocol for the Internet of Trust - Conceptual Whitepaper (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3266953
scope_conditions: Semada platform block propagation

subjectOf.text: A blockchain guarantee means that a contract between principal and agent executes only if and when all contract parameters have been fulfilled by both parties and verified by a majority of miners or nodes in the system.
subjectOf.abstract: Blockchain guarantees include contract execution between principal and agent only if and when all contract parameters were fulfilled by both parties and verified by a majority of miners/nodes in the system.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393

subjectOf.text: The distributed consensus model, in which network nodes verify and validate transactions before execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain, and it does so without compromising the privacy of the parties.
subjectOf.abstract: Blockchains' distributed consensus model, e.g. the network "nodes" verify and validate chain transactions before transaction execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393

subjectOf.text: The interoperability deficit in cryptocurrency markets is partly intrinsic to blockchain technology itself, because the consensus mechanism that allows block propagation on one chain in some ways negates interoperability with other chains and their consensus.
subjectOf.abstract: The lack of interoperability can in part be traced back to blockchain technology itself. The consensus created to allow block propagation in some ways negates interoperability with other chains and their consensus.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

subjectOf.text: The double spending problem has not been eradicated in theory: a group or syndicate obtaining 51 percent control of a network could reverse transactions and create a private chain that the market could only limitedly discern as not real.
subjectOf.abstract: There is the possibility a group or syndicate could gain 51% control over the network and would therefore be able to reverse transactions and create a private blockchain, which the market could only limitedly discern as not real.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: a decentralized network where one party can amass majority hashing control

subjectOf.text: The data mining that produces scarcity in existing blockchains also slows creation, so high speed transactions cannot be achieved for the foreseeable future without a different consensus design.
subjectOf.abstract: Currently, the data mining required to provide scarcity also slows creation so that high speed transactions cannot be achieved for the foreseeable future.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - Past, Present, and Future (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411897
scope_conditions: proof of work style mining that manufactures scarcity

subjectOf.text: The tradeoff between transaction approval speed and immutability has the potential to undermine the DeFi infrastructure in the long run.
subjectOf.abstract: The trade-off between transaction approval speed and immutability has the potential to undermine the DeFi infrastructure in the long run.
subjectOf.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: consensus based decentralized ledgers supporting DeFi

subjectOf.text: Consensus in decentralized systems presents a two sided cost problem: creating consensus raises the costs of prepping, processing, and storing information, while reducing the number of computational checks increases the risk of collusion attacks that could change the record.
subjectOf.abstract: Creating consensus requires increase costs of prepping, processing, and storing information.333 On the other hand, fewer computational checks for consensus increase the risk of collusion attacks that could change the record.
subjectOf.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: public distributed consensus systems
information distributed to and validated by all parties

subjectOf.text: Because individual network nodes verify and validate transactions before execution under the distributed consensus model, recording a fraudulent transaction on the blockchain is extremely rare.
subjectOf.abstract: The distributed consensus model, individual network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before the execution of the transactions, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
subjectOf.citation: Kaal, Blockchain Technology for Good (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3709041
scope_conditions: requires a distributed consensus model with independent node validation

subjectOf.text: Hash functions let a leaderless network reach consensus on identity and ordering, because every node independently hashes a transaction's data and deterministically arrives at the same unique identifier that everyone recognizes.
subjectOf.abstract: Thanks to the hash function, every node in the network hashes the transaction's data and independently arrives at the same an- swer, giving the transaction a unique ID that everyone recognizes.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: requires all nodes to run the same deterministic hash protocol

subjectOf.text: Proof of stake carries an unresolved failure mode: if anyone devises a clever algorithm for hijacking the block producer selection process, the network would fail.
subjectOf.abstract: The problem is that if someone comes up with a clever algorithm for hijacking the process, then the network would fail.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to proof of stake designs that select block producers pseudorandomly

subjectOf.text: Because a group sometimes genuinely has no consensus to be discovered, network forking is at times inevitable rather than a governance failure that better rules could prevent.
subjectOf.abstract: First, that is a major problem for democracy. Sometimes there is no consensus to be had. This leads to the second conclusion that sometimes network forking is inevitable.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: cyclic or irreconcilable group preferences
decentralized networks whose members can exit

subjectOf.text: Bitcoin's proof of work has produced no protocol violation in more than a decade, meaning no rule breaking message has been incorporated into the finalized blockchain, even though anyone can run a hacked version of the algorithm anonymously at any time.
subjectOf.abstract: Despite the fact that anyone can run any hacked version of the algo- rithm at any time from an anonymous account, there has not been a single protocol violation—meaning no message has been incorporated in the finalized blockchain which breaks the rules of the algorithm.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: Bitcoin proof of work as of 2021
network of millions of users

subjectOf.text: Loosely coupled voting, in which staked reputation cannot be lost, encourages dissenting opinions, while tightly coupled voting, in which losing stakes are redistributed, guarantees consensus; a DAO steers deliberation by moving between the two.
subjectOf.abstract: Loosely-coupled voting encourages dissenting opinions. Tightly-coupled voting guarantees consensus.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Governance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782214
scope_conditions: reputation weighted validation pools

subjectOf.text: Maintaining consensus without a central authority forces a reputation system to verify members' votes extremely redundantly, which imposes serious computational overhead.
subjectOf.abstract: In order to maintain consensus in a decentralized network, with no central authority to check in with, a reputational system needs to verify each others' votes extremely redundantly, which leads to serious overhead costs in computation.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Finance (DeFi) (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782216
scope_conditions: decentralized networks with no central authority

subjectOf.text: Proof of Work block rewards structurally reintroduce centralization: the economic nature of mining rewards incentivizes degrees of centralization through collective action of nodes that share rewards as a group, that is, mining pools.
subjectOf.abstract: The economic nature of these rewards incentivizes degrees of centralization in collective action of nodes that share in the mining rewards as a group, so called mining pools.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: Proof of Work consensus with block rewards
Bitcoin in the early 2020s

subjectOf.text: Decentralized governance structures impose their own costs: with no central authority to coordinate diverse stakeholders, consensus is difficult to reach, negotiations are prolonged, and enforcement of agreements is weak because no single entity is responsible for compliance.
subjectOf.abstract: In decentralized systems, the lack of a central authority often leads to difficulties in coordinating and achieving consensus among diverse stakeholders, each with their own priorities and objectives. This can result in prolonged negotiations or weak enforcement of agreements
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to decentralized structures without a coordinating authority
evidenced in the paper by the environmental agreement domain

subjectOf.text: In traditional federated learning environments the reliability of updates arriving from various nodes is hard to establish; web3 smart contracts and consensus mechanisms can automate that verification at the point of aggregation.
subjectOf.abstract: In traditional FL environments, ensuring the reliability of updates from various nodes can be challenging. Web3's smart contracts and consensus mechanisms can automate the verification of updates from participating nodes
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: federated learning with untrusted or unverified participating nodes

subjectOf.text: Validation pools evaluate contributions democratically on the basis of staked tokens, and the outcome of that evaluation governs the minting of new reputation tokens, so community consensus on AI decisions is what determines standing in the system.
subjectOf.abstract: Validation Pools allow for the democratic evaluation of contributions based on staked tokens, with outcomes influencing the minting of new REP tokens that reflect community consensus on AI-related decisions.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: the proposed web3 community governance architecture

subjectOf.text: Distributing governance across all participants prevents any single entity from dominating decision making, and because model or training changes then require consensus, the resulting decisions reflect collective rather than individual interest.
subjectOf.abstract: By distributing governance across all participants, the proposed web3 community governance system ensures that no single entity can dominate the decision-making process. This structure promotes the alignment of incentives since changes to the model or the training process require consensus
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: governance systems where change requires consensus among distributed participants

subjectOf.text: When decision making power is distributed across multiple entities in a federated model, consensus and cooperation become harder to reach, which makes cohesive AI governance mechanisms difficult to establish.
subjectOf.abstract: In a federated model, where decision-making power is distributed across multiple entities, it becomes harder to achieve consensus and cooperation, making it challenging to establish cohesive AI governance mechanisms.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance Via Web3 Reputation System (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4941807
scope_conditions: where governance authority is distributed across multiple independent entities

subjectOf.text: Validation Pools are the consensus mechanism of the proposed system: an author's stakes are pooled to evaluate a specific forum post, and the outcome of the pool can mint new reputation tokens that reflect community consensus on that contribution.
subjectOf.abstract: Validation Pool (VP) form a crucial mechanism where an author's stakes are pooled to evaluate specific posts within the forum. The outcome of a VP can lead to the minting of new REP tokens, reflecting the consensus on a given issue or contribution.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance Via Web3 Reputation System (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4941807
scope_conditions: where participants stake against specific forum posts

subjectOf.text: Making governance decisions collectively through web3 consensus minimizes bias and single points of failure, because oversight is no longer subject to the limitations or errors of a solitary AI system.
subjectOf.abstract: decentralized approach minimizes the risk of bias and single points of failure, as governance decisions are made collectively rather than being subject to the limitations or potential errors of a solitary AI system.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How can we Best Monitor AI Agents (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5245185
scope_conditions: consensus driven decision making among diverse stakeholders

subjectOf.text: The weighted Borda count consensus mechanism preserves the 2018 framework's security property that fifty one percent good faith participation ensures correct outcomes, while extending it to richer quality assessment.
subjectOf.abstract: This theorem establishes that the revised framework preserves the security property from Calcaterra, Kaal, and Andrei (2018) that 51% good-faith participation ensures correct outcomes, while extending it to richer quality assessment.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Domain-Specific Reputation Systems From Binary Validation to Citation-Weighted Knowledge Attribution (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6192998
scope_conditions: validator votes weighted by reputation stake
a stake weighted majority of validators is honest

subjectOf.text: Validators who align with the stake weighted consensus ranking gain reputation and those who deviate lose it, which carries the winner takes losers' stakes property of the original framework over to ranked voting.
subjectOf.abstract: Validators who align with consensus gain reputation. Those who deviate lose it. Thus, preserving the winner-takes-losers'-stakes property from the original framework (Calcaterra, Kaal, and Andrei 2018, 7) while extending it to ranked voting.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Domain-Specific Reputation Systems From Binary Validation to Citation-Weighted Knowledge Attribution (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6192998
scope_conditions: validator agreement measured by normalized Kendall tau distance from consensus
